item.title: TCM diagnostic device travels to space, using digitalized methods to bring health checks to taikonauts
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 17:13:00
Taikonauts aboard the Shenzhou-23 crew use a TCM diagnostic device to monitor their health. Photo: CCTV News A traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) diagnostic device made another appearance aboard China's space station recently, where it monitors the health of the taikonauts, CCTV News reported on Wednesday. The device digitizes the four fundamental diagnostic methods of TCM - inspection, auscultation and olfaction, inquiry, and palpation. Rooted in centuries-old TCM practice, the approach can now also be applied in space to help assess the health of the taikonauts, according to an updated Tiangong work vlog. Since the Shenzhou-12 mission in 2021, the TCM diagnostic device has been served aboard China's space station as a health-monitoring tool for taikonauts. During examinations, taikonauts collect data on their tongue, facial features and pulse, which is transmitted to ground-based medical personnel for analysis and comparison, allowing health assessments to be conducted from Earth, per the CCTV report. Through a viewing window, the device precisely captures images of the taikonaut's tongue, detecting subtle features for health assessment by the medical team on the ground. It can also capture facial images, recording features such as facial complexion and expression for further analysis. For pulse diagnosis, a dedicated pulse-sensing unit records the taikonaut's pulse information. The device's internal software system then compares the pulse data with theoretical models of TCM pulse patterns, simulating the traditional practice of "taking the pulse," CCTV reported. The device also includes a medical questionnaire, which taikonauts complete while in orbit to report their own subjective health experiences. The questionnaire responses are combined with tongue, facial, and pulse data to create a comprehensive health profile for each taikonaut. During spaceflight, taikonauts face lots of challenges such as microgravity and space radiation, which can lead to changes in physiological rhythms and other health-related effects. Therefore, continuous health monitoring is essential, the media report noted. TCM-based diagnosis can help assess taikonauts' overall functional status and provide early warning of potential health changes. To bring the device into space, there are a series of challenges posed by the complex space station environment. In 2010, a team participated in the multinational Mars500 program. Over the 520-day experiment, they collected data from 37 rounds of TCM four-diagnosis assessments. The data showed that health assessments based on TCM diagnostic information were largely consistent with other health-monitoring data, indicating that the device can objectively reflect taikonauts' health status and laying the groundwork for its deployment aboard the space station. Because conditions in space differ greatly from those on the Earth, and the space environment is highly complex, diagnostic standards used on the ground cannot simply be applied in orbit. The Chinese team, therefore, conducted extensive simulation experiments and scientifically designed the measurement parameters for tongue, facial and pulse diagnosis, CCTV reported. Starting from scratch, they established objective standards and a corresponding database for TCM diagnosis in spaceflight, said the report. One advantage of this system is its simplicity for long-term health monitoring of taikonauts in space, Wang Yanan, chief editor of Aerospace Knowledge magazine, told the Global Times on Wednesday. It requires neither blood sampling nor additional sensors, and involves no complex procedures such as chemical testing. Instead, the monitoring process relies on methods including image acquisition, making it relatively simple and convenient to implement, Wang said. These data and findings could also contribute to enriching the theory and practice of TCM, Wang said, potentially helping further advance and strengthen the field.

item.title: Indonesia reportedly expects Chinese J-10 fighter jets within six months; air force chief of staff urges public patience
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 17:10:00
Two J-10 fighter jets attached to an aviation brigade with the air force under the Chinese PLA Southern Theater Command taxi on the runway after returning from a nighttime flight training exercise in recent days. (eng.chinamil.com.cn/Photo by Xiao Rui) Indonesia's Air Force Chief of Staff reportedly told the public recently to be patient about the delivery of J-10 fighter jets from China, with an Indonesian media report saying the Chinese-made warplanes are expected to arrive in Indonesia within six months. An expert said the J-10CE fighter jet has attracted interest from several countries since its reported combat performance in May last year, thanks to its combat-proven capabilities and high cost-effectiveness. Indonesian Air Force Chief of Staff (KSAU) Air Marshal Mohamad Tonny Harjono asked the public to be patient regarding the arrival of Chengdu J-10 fighter jets from China, Indonesian media outlet Republika reported on Tuesday. "Just wait," Tonny was quoted by Republika as saying at the TNI Headquarters, Cilangkap, East Jakarta on Monday. Republika, citing its own information, reported that the fighter jets nicknamed the Vigorous Dragon are expected to arrive in Indonesia six months from now. However, the number of units arriving in Indonesia for the first time next year is still unknown. At the same location, a member of Commission I of the Indonesian House of Representatives supported the Indonesian Ministry of Defense's move to purchase J-10 fighter jets. He considered purchasing 4.5-generation fighter jets from China could strengthen the defense of the country, according to the Republika report. In October 2025, Indonesia's Minister of Defense Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin confirmed that Indonesia is set to acquire Chengdu J-10 fighter jets from China, Indonesian news agency Antara reported at the time. In response to a related question, Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesperson for the Ministry of National Defense, said at a regular press conference in October 2025 that China has always taken a prudent and responsible attitude toward the export of military equipment. "We are willing to share the new achievements of our equipment development with peace-loving countries and jointly safeguard international and regional peace and stability," the spokesperson said. Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times that the J-10CE has drawn significant international attention after it has reportedly demonstrated its capabilities in the air combat between Pakistan and India in May 2025. One of the highlights of the J-10CE is its beyond-visual-range air combat capabilities when paired with the PL-15 series of air-to-air missiles. With the aircraft's outstanding radar detection capability, the PL-15 missile's range could be fully utilized, giving it an advantage in securing air superiority, Zhang said. The expert also noted that the J-10CE offers high cost-effectiveness, being more affordable than Western fighters of comparable capability. In August, Uzbek state media unveiled Chinese J-10CE fighters during the country's national celebration. O'zbekiston 24, a channel under Uzbekistan's state television and radio company, broadcast the event live. The released footage showed six J-10CE fighters being welcomed with a traditional water salute after landing. The aircraft bore the markings of the Uzbek military, Newshub.uz reported. Uzbekistan thus became the second confirmed overseas customer of the J-10CE, after Pakistan. Observers called this a breakthrough for advanced Chinese fighter jets in the international market, particularly in Central Asia. At the sixth Azerbaijan International Defense Exhibition, which opened at the Baku Expo Center on September 30 local time, the J-10CE fighter jet was among a range of Chinese-made aircraft being showcased. According to a photo released by Aviation Industry Corporation of China (AVIC), a model of a J-10CE was displayed with the national flag of Azerbaijan, with Zhang telling Global Times in a previous interview that it could suggest growing recognition of the fighter jet on the Azerbaijani side and raise the possibility that the two sides could eventually reach a procurement agreement. Bangladesh is also reportedly advancing plans to purchase Chinese-made J-10CE fighter jets. Bloomberg reported in August that a government negotiating committee had finalized a draft contract for the procurement of the multi-role combat aircraft. Bangladeshi media outlet Daily Sabah also reported that draft agreements covering the J-10CE and attack helicopters had been prepared and submitted to relevant authorities for approval.

item.title: China's railway passenger trips surpass 250 million as National Day holiday ends
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 11:25:00
Passengers prepare to board a train at Nanjing South Railway Station in Nanjing, east China's Jiangsu Province, Sept. 30, 2026. China's railway network saw a peak in passenger flow on Wednesday, one day before the beginning of the seven-day National Day holiday. Photo: Xinhua China's railways recorded more than 250 million passenger trips from September 23 to Tuesday, as the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day breaks wrap up, China State Railway Group Co said on Wednesday. Wednesday marks the final day of China's National Day holiday, with the railway operator to handle 24.15 million passenger trips. Starting from Tuesday, the railway witnessed a marked increase in return passenger traffic, according to the state railway operator. To cope with the peak demand, a total of 2,449 passenger train services will be added on Wednesday. Railway operators planned to add 169.5 pairs of passenger train services to destinations including Harbin, Shenyang and Dalian in Northeast China and Datong in North China's Shanxi Province, CCTV News reported, citing China Railway Beijing Group. The company expected passenger volume to rise by 15 percent year-on-year. Besides, China Railway Shanghai Group expects to handle 4.15 million passenger trips on Wednesday, including 210 nighttime bullet train services to meet passengers' demand for timely return travel. In Guangzhou, the local railway operator expects a spike of 20.8 percent in passenger numbers. A total of 765 train services are scheduled to be added to destinations including Beijing, cities in the Pearl River Delta and Yangtze River Delta. China's sprawling high-speed railway network, the world's largest, is one of the key areas highlighting the country's transportation strengths and economic vitality. On September 28, China opened four major high-speed railway sections across northern, northwestern, central and northeastern China, with a combined length of more than 1,100 kilometers, according to reports.

item.title: New professions show China's industrial, livelihood progress
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-07 07:25:00
A drone monitors an agricultural demonstration park in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province, Sept. 18, 2026. (Xinhua/Lu Jinbo) A stream of new occupations is emerging at the forefront of China's new technologies, industries and business models, mirroring industrial upgrading and improvements in people's livelihoods. In the low-altitude economy sector alone, newly added positions such as drone swarm flight planners, low-altitude logistics specialists, and low-altitude intelligent connected system administrators stand out in the eighth batch of new professions recently released by the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security and other government departments. Occupations tied to the booming digital economy are also reshaping work in China, including AI engineering technicians, intelligent connected vehicle testers, embodied intelligent robot application technicians, and microgrid administrators, among others. The release of 11 new occupations and 23 new job types in the eighth batch marks a fresh update to the country's occupational catalog. Such updates serve as a talent "barometer" reflecting the pulse of China's industrial transformation, industry insiders noted. Take the low-altitude economy for example. The first batch of new occupations, released in 2019, introduced the drone pilots to meet the urgent demand for drone operations. The second batch added drone assembly and maintenance technicians, a role created to close the gap in equipment operation and maintenance for the emerging drone industry. As the drone industry has grown, new positions in the seventh and eighth batches have taken on responsibilities that expand from single technical operations to cross-cutting application fields such as logistics delivery, cultural tourism operations, and urban governance. The continuous release of new occupations reflects China's industrial system moving toward higher-end, smarter and greener development, said Li Qiang, vice president of online job-seeking platform Zhaopin. "Policy support expands and underpins the talent supply, while the job market absorbs in tandem. New occupations are both a precise mapping of the industrial development trends and a positive guide for the talent market," Li said. An employee operates a humanoid robot to repair electrical equipment at an embodied AI training base in Beijing, capital of China, on May 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liwang) Beyond industrial upgrading, changes in China's new occupations also reflect evolving demands in people's livelihoods, with new jobs in the modern services sector continuing to expand. Industry insiders noted that as people's quality of life has been improving, producer services have moved toward specialization and the higher end of the value chain, while consumer services have developed toward higher quality, greater diversity, and convenience. The size of China's service sector is expected to expand beyond 100 trillion yuan (about 14.8 trillion U.S. dollars) in the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), according to the National Development and Reform Commission, the country's top economic planner. Industry insiders say the consumer services sector will be explored to unlock economic growth potential, with broad scope for developing residential services, health services, aged care, and childcare. Therefore, progress in this sector is expected to generate even more new jobs. China has been dynamically updating its occupational classification catalog. Since 2019, the country has issued eight batches of 121 new occupations. In 2020, the second batch introduced health-related new professions including healthcare attendants and rehabilitation assistive technology consultants. Subsequent batches continued this momentum, adding niche occupations and job types such as ski patrol rescuers, family education instructors, age-friendly renovation designers, and incense-making artisans. China's State Council has issued a plan to implement the employment-first strategy during the 15th Five-Year Plan period, calling for stronger synergy among macroeconomic policies on employment and highlighting efforts to stabilize employment in labor-intensive industries, expand employment in the service sector, and tap employment potential in emerging fields. "The emergence of new occupations is a direct response to new applications of technologies, fresh market changes, and new consumer demands," said Li Chang'an, a researcher at the Academy of China Open Economy Studies under the University of International Business and Economics. "Every update of the occupational catalog will inject more talent-driven momentum into the country's industrial development in the future alongside the advancement of the occupational standard system, alignment between talent cultivation and supply, and rules and systems to safeguard the progress of the sector," Li added.

item.title: 20-plus Chinese nationals fleeing Myanmar scam compound shot at close range with AK-47s, CCTV documentary reveals
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06 14:50:00
A screenshot of the documentary The Demise of Myanmar-Based Telecom Fraud. Source: CCTV official weibo account A Chinese documentary has revealed details of a deadly shooting in Myanmar in which more than 20 Chinese nationals attempting to flee a telecom fraud compound were intercepted by armed Myanmar nationals and shot at close range with AK-47 assault rifles, leaving six dead and eight injured. The incident took place on August 5, 2023, according to The Demise of Myanmar-Based Telecom Fraud, a documentary jointly produced by China’s Ministry of Public Security and China Media Group. It is scheduled to air on China Central Television (CCTV) from Monday to Wednesday. The Chinese nationals had been working in a scam compound and decided to flee after being subjected to violent coercion, according to the documentary. “We firmly believed we could make it out. We could return to China,” a survivor surnamed Wu recalled. “What we didn’t expect was that they opened fire directly.” The armed personnel at the compound blocked the group as they attempted to escape and opened fire with AK-47 assault rifles at close range. The shooting continued for about 10 seconds, Wu said. Some of the victims were seriously mutilated by the gunfire, according to the documentary. Chinese police said their investigation identified a businessman named Lin Jian as the person who ordered the shooting. According to the documentary, Lin had obtained control of 30 Chinese nationals from Tenglong, a company associated with the Bai family, one of the four major criminal gangs in northern Myanmar, and brought them under his company, called Jinxin, where they were involved in investment fraud under a profit-sharing arrangement. Investigators found traces of blood that appeared to have been cleaned from parts of the compound. They also extracted biological material from bullet fragments. The forensic evidence helped confirm the direction of the investigation, according to Chinese police. With the assistance of law enforcement authorities in Myanmar, six Myanmar nationals accused of taking part in the shooting and burying the bodies, along with Lin, were apprehended between January and July 2024, according to the documentary. The documentary, which chronicles China's efforts to fight against telecom fraud networks in northern Myanmar, also details the efforts to dismantle the four major criminal groups known in the region as the “four major families.” The three-episode documentary series offers an unprecedented look into the horrific reality of Myanmar cyber fraud networks, as well as China’s determination and relentless crackdown on notorious cross-border cyber-scam operations. Global Times

item.title: China's modernization report card: Why does the West keep asking 'who pays'?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06 13:22:00
A view of Shanghai Photo: VCG Every nation wants modernization. For a long time, the West saw itself as the frontrunner, convinced that its path was the universal model. But when China achieved in decades what had taken Western industrial powers centuries, some Western elites grew uneasy. At first, they dismissed China’s progress. Then, when China’s achievements became impossible to ignore, they raised a loaded question: What is the “cost” of Chinese modernization and who pays? The implication is clear: China’s rise must have come at someone else’s expense – an absurd claim that deserves a closer look. A zero-sum view behind the ‘cost’ question In many ways, the West’s “China cost theory” reflects its own experience of modernization. Western industrialization was accompanied by slavery, colonial plunder, wars for hegemony and severe environmental damage. These experiences shaped a collective memory in which modernization was seen as a process of conquest, extraction and the sacrifice of other countries. From that perspective, one country’s rise means another’s fall. The irony is that this logic, derived from Western history, is being projected onto China by the West, which places itself on the moral high ground, demanding that China “answer” for its rise while assuming that its own development is exempt from judgment. The question of “who pays” is not only a sign of self-righteous arrogance. It also reflects a deeper anxiety. If China’s model proves effective, then what the West has long claimed as universal values and the ultimate model for modernization and governance will be significantly weakened. China’s answer: facts, confidence and candor Instead of blindly copying foreign models, China has forged its own path to modernization – one that does not rely on plundering others, exporting domestic problems or waiting for handouts. It is the result of generations of hard work and determined pursuit by the Chinese people. There is nothing to hide, and nothing to fear. Development does involve costs. But China’s costs are not borne at another’s expense. They are the pains of industrial upgrading, ecological restoration and conservation, and the strenuous work of grassroots governance. They are the costs of transforming the economy, improving people’s lives and pursuing long-term development without following the old path of sacrificing other countries. China has phased out polluting and low-efficiency industrial capacity in pursuit of green, high-quality development. In resource-based cities that face the pressure of slower growth and job transfers, workers receive retraining and basic unemployment support. In that process, all stakeholders – from governments and enterprises to workers – have shared the burden of transition. Hundreds of millions of migrant workers have left their hometowns to help build cities. Technical professionals have gone to the front lines of industry. Many officials and public servants have worked in remote and difficult areas to narrow development gaps. When economic growth conflicts with food security or ecological protection, China does not judge success by GDP figures alone. It has held the red line of 1.8 billion mu (about 120 million hectares) of arable land, strengthened ecological security and built a firmer foundation for long-term national development. Modernization measured by people’s happiness Chinese modernization represents a different form of governance than Western electoral politics. It is not measured by capital returns or stock market indices. Putting people front and center, it is all about whether ordinary households can lead safe, healthy and happy lives. When Chinese people travel across the country on high-speed trains, go out at night without security concerns, make cashless payments, and enjoy quick, easy access to affordable medical services at community hospitals and warm meals at neighborhood canteens, they are reaping the tangible fruits of Chinese modernization. Beyond a singular model of modernization Chinese modernization at its core is about balanced development and shared progress. It does not seek to threaten or supersede anyone, it only aims to meet the people’s growing demand for a more prosperous life. China’s development path is winning recognition from more people around the world, especially in the Global South – not only because it has lifted China to where it stands today, but because it is helping other countries rise alongside it. China is a major contributor to global growth, peace and stability, a strong partner in the global energy transition, and a key provider of digital infrastructure, enabling fellow developing countries to join the fast track of digital development. As China continues to offer more public goods to the world, it is only natural that more countries will view China’s development positively. There is no singular or fixed answer to the question of how to achieve modernization. China’s development offers the Global South not only an alternative path, but also greater space to pursue development on its own terms. China may be a latecomer to modernization, but it is a genuine trailblazer. Modernization should be a process of shared progress, not a contest in which one side maintains its lead by holding another back. The author is a commentator on international affairs, writing regularly for Xinhua News, Global Times, China Daily, CGTN, etc. He can be reached at shaoxia2019@163.com.

item.title: China rebukes certain Western countries over human rights criticism, says they have no right to lecture it
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-06 12:38:00
Photo: VCG Sun Lei, China’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the United Nations, on Tuesday delivered a rebuttal during the general debate of the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in response to Western countries, urging a handful of countries to stop fabricating and spreading lies about China and stop using human rights issues for political manipulation. China strongly condemns and is firmly opposed to the groundless accusations and malicious smears of China’s human rights situation made by countries including the UK, Australia, Japan, Ireland, the Czech Republic and Lithuania, in their replies during the general debate of the Third Committee of the United Nations General Assembly, Sun said, according to a statement released by the Permanent Mission of China to the UN on Tuesday. These countries consider themselves superior to others and often assume the posture of self-appointed “human rights teachers,” yet they have serious human rights problems of their own, Sun said, adding that these countries are in no position to lecture others on human rights, let alone make irresponsible remarks about China. According to Sun, China has continued to safeguard and improve people’s well-being through development, eliminating absolute poverty nationwide. Nearly 100 million people have been lifted out of impoverishment, and a middle-income group of more than 400 million people has been established. By contrast, poverty has continued to worsen in the UK in recent years, with over 14 million people living below the poverty line, half of whom are in “extreme poverty.” In Japan, the relative poverty rate among households stands at 15 percent, while child poverty has become increasingly pronounced. China expresses deep concern over the human rights situations in Japan, Sun said. Meanwhile, China has continued to advance whole-process people’s democracy and ensure that the people run the country, with public support for and satisfaction with the government exceeding 90 percent for years. The national security law in Hong Kong marked a historic turning point for Hong Kong, bringing it from chaos to governance and from stability to prosperity, while improving and developing its democratic system, winning broad support across the city, Sun said. By contrast, polls show that about 75 percent of people in the UK are concerned about the future of democracy. In Australia and the Czech Republic, public trust in government has fallen to new lows, with young people’s confidence in democracy also declining significantly, Sun added. Sun said that all ethnic groups in China are equal members of the family of the Chinese nation and are closely united like the seeds of a pomegranate. The political, economic, cultural, religious and other rights of people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region and Xizang Autonomous Region are effectively protected. The enactment and implementation of the Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law aims to promote common prosperity and development among all ethnic groups. By contrast, Japan has failed to fulfill its commitments to eliminate racial discrimination and has not treated the Ainu and Ryukyu peoples as equal ethnic groups, leaving their survival and development under threat. In the UK, Australia and Ireland, colonialism has caused enduring harm to this day, and these countries are facing serious social problems, including racism and ethnic divisions, Sun said. Sun said that amid global turbulence and headwinds facing multilateralism, China has contributed to the international human rights cause through its development and concrete efforts to promote dialogue, cooperation and more equitable global human rights governance. By contrast, countries such as the UK, Australia, Japan, the Czech Republic and Lithuania frequently invoke morality, yet remain indifferent to the unjust treatment suffered by the people of Palestine, Iran and Cuba. They repeatedly use human rights as a pretext to interfere in the internal affairs of other countries and impose unilateral coercive measures, infringing on the interests of developing countries and playing a highly disgraceful role, Sun added. Sun said the global trend toward multipolarity and more democratic international relations is irreversible and called for greater solidarity and cooperation on human rights. He said that China would pursue a human rights development path suited to its national conditions, engage in constructive dialogue and oppose the politicization of human rights, while urging a small number of countries to stop fabricating and spreading lies about China and stop using human rights issues for political manipulation. Otherwise, they will only end up hurting themselves. Global Times

item.title: Tokyo expresses 'regret,' lodges protest over a US Marine killing in Okinawa. Then what?
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-05 19:35:00
People hold a march calling for the burden on Okinawa from hosting US forces to be lifted in Okinawa on May 14, 2022. Photo: VCG A US service member causes a tragedy on Japanese soil. Japan expresses "regret," lodges a "strong protest," and demands measures to "prevent a recurrence." The US says it will fully cooperate with the investigation. The language is strong. The tone is grave. And then what? The bases remain. Military aircraft keep taking off and landing. The military buildup continues. When the next case comes, Tokyo will go through much the same script. This time, the victim is 39-year-old Anna Yagi, who died in a hotel in Naha, Okinawa. Next time, who will it be? A US Marine was arrested Sunday on suspicion of murder and robbery after Yagi's body was discovered in a hotel room in Okinawa. Reports cited police as saying that Yagi had "died from suffocation after being strangled." The case prompted outrage across Japan, and the Japanese government was compelled to put on a show of anger. The Japanese government quickly started an almost predictable crisis-response routine: Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned the US ambassador; Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi lodged a protest with the commander of US Forces Japan; and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi expressed regret on social media and demanded that the US military tighten discipline on October 4. A day later, before her policy speech in the House of Representatives, she said it again: the crime was "extremely regrettable." Japan had lodged a strong protest, she added, and demanded full cooperation, stricter discipline, and measures to prevent a recurrence. The question is: What actually changes when Japan repeats the same words again and again? Take a look at the numbers. According to police figures cited in reports, Okinawa police cleared 6,235 criminal cases involving US service members, base employees, and their relatives from 1972 to 2023. Of these, 586 were serious offenses, including murder, robbery, and sexual assault. In 2024, a US serviceman was sentenced to five years for kidnapping and raping a Japanese schoolgirl. The Japanese side stressed the need to take measures to prevent a recurrence. Yet similar cases followed. A total of 101 criminal charges were filed against US military personnel and others connected to the US military in Okinawa Prefecture in 2025, according to prefectural police. It was the first time in 22 years - since 2003 - that the tentative figure had surpassed 100. The promise is always the same: tighten discipline, prevent a recurrence. Yet the crimes are not. What, then, do the promises mean? Perhaps the most disturbing thing is not whether any one protest was strong enough. It is how familiar the sequence has become. The same pattern repeats again and again. For Tokyo, the US-Japan alliance is a so-called national security imperative. For Washington, it is a regional strategy. For ordinary people in Okinawa, it is first of all the place where they live. For years, they have experienced the alliance as noise, accidents, crime, military bases, and the constant worry of not knowing what will happen next. On October 4, Okinawa's newly elected governor, Genta Koja, told reporters that the fact that this kind of event has happened again leaves us no choice but to conclude that the US military's efforts in maintaining discipline, educating personnel, and other such measures are completely ineffective. On October 5, Japanese media quoted former upper house member Keiko Itokazu as saying that Okinawans, especially women, should not have to keep bearing this grief and pain. She said that each time, the Japanese government and the US military have claimed to impose stricter discipline and provide proper education for service members. "Is this the result of the so-called education?" she asked, warning that if the bases expand and the number of US troops grows, the harm is likely to grow. In Western foreign-policy discourse, "ally" is a common word. It suggests equality, respect, and mutual support. But who is kept safe? Who carries the risk? Who decides where that risk falls? And who is allowed to say no? Those are the questions that word should bring into the open. That is also why a criminal case can eventually become a political mirror. In that mirror, there is certainly the individual responsibility of the US service member involved. But there is also Japan's own choice. Some observers have therefore argued that Japan's protests are largely for show. Okinawa is home to more than 40 US military bases, about 70 percent of all the US bases in Japan. In recent years, despite sustained local opposition, Tokyo has continued to expand both its own military presence and the US footprint there. Step by step, the prefecture is being turned into a forward bastion. The US-Japan Status of Forces Agreement was signed in 1960. Under Article 17, the US has primary jurisdiction when service members commit crimes in the performance of official duty. Whether an act is deemed to have been committed in the performance of official duty is largely determined by the US side. On August 20, 2026, the governors of 15 prefectures with US bases petitioned Tokyo for a fundamental revision of the agreement. But so far, public reporting has shown no commitment to revise it. Repeated crimes by US military personnel have been met with the same promises and little visible change. Many cases involving US military personnel in Japan have gone unresolved. That is part of the situation Okinawa lives with today. The contradiction is familiar. The number of crimes remains high. The bases have not moved. Protest has become a form of diplomatic theater. It raises a hard question: is Tokyo trying to solve Okinawa's problem, or only to manage Okinawa's anger about it? A woman is dead in a hotel in Naha. Her name was Anna Yagi. Her death is likely, sooner or later, to be overtaken by the next case involving US personnel and become another line in Okinawa's long record of such harm. The Japanese government will probably issue another statement of "strong protest." Sometimes, this is what being an ally looks like.

item.title: The more turbulent the world becomes, the more precious a peaceful China is: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-30 00:27:00
A night view of the Wangfujing pedestrian street in Beijing on September 27, 2026. Photo: VCG Peace and security are defining features of China's governance and hallmarks of Chinese modernization. Peaceful China is a light that millions upon millions of Chinese people, secure in their daily lives, shine into a world that is far from peaceful. It safeguards the everyday lives of millions of families while contributing Chinese wisdom, Chinese solutions and Chinese strength to global security governance. A working conference on the Peaceful China Initiative was held in Beijing on Monday. A recent instruction made by Chinese President Xi Jinping was conveyed at the conference. In his instruction, Xi stated that since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, significant progress has been made in building a safe China, making the country one of the safest in the world. Notably, peace and security are defining features of China's governance and hallmarks of Chinese modernization. Throughout human history, no country or region has achieved modernization amid persistent turmoil. From the development of a nation to the well-being of every family, peace and security are indispensable. China now ranks among the countries with the lowest rates of criminal offenses and homicide and the fewest gun-related crimes. These three distinctions provide a solid foundation for the strong sense of security enjoyed by the Chinese people. Advancing the Peaceful China Initiative in a turbulent and rapidly changing world represents a weighty commitment. The 2026 Global Peace Index shows that global peacefulness has deteriorated for 12 consecutive years, while the number of active state-based conflicts worldwide has reached its highest level since the end of World War II. According to the latest report from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, as of the end of 2025, there were 117 million people forcibly displaced globally, equivalent to one in every 67 people on Earth. Meanwhile, Gallup's 2025 Global Safety Report showed that among 144 countries and regions surveyed, 94 percent of respondents in China said they feel safe walking alone at night. China has once again been recognized as one of the safest countries in the world and is the only major world power to make the list. In today's world, stability itself has become a scarce resource, and it is widely recognized as one of China's strengths. When foreign bloggers and visitors come to China, what often surprises them most is not the high-speed rail network or spectacular drone light shows, but the small details of everyday life that directly affect them: being able to go out for a late-night meal at 1 am, having a taxi driver return a phone left in the car, leaving a backpack at a café table while ordering and finding it still there upon returning, or seeing a young woman finish work, take the subway and then a bus, before walking another 10 minutes through a hutong or alley to get home. Scenes that might require suspenseful background music in an urban drama elsewhere are simply part of ordinary life in China. Data from China's National Immigration Administration showed that inbound trips made by foreign nationals exceeded 22.91 million in the first half of 2026, a surge of 20.4 percent year-on-year. There is a close connection between China's favorable public security environment and the continuing popularity of "China Travel." What particularly impresses many foreign visitors is that in China, security is not a privilege enjoyed by a small minority, but a basic public good accessible to the Chinese people. A peaceful China is no accident. It is the result of a combination of factors, including institutional strengths, governance effectiveness, cultural traditions and economic development. China's approach to security is people-centered, with development at its core. Poverty alleviation, medical insurance, social security, compulsory education and employment support all help give people confidence that their lives can continue to improve. From pushing to dismantle the "four major families" of criminal rings in northern Myanmar to better safeguarding food safety; from cracking down in accordance with the law on crimes targeting the elderly and children to continuously strengthening the public security prevention and control system; and from resolving disputes at their source to identifying and addressing public safety hazards, the advancement of the Peaceful China Initiative has continuously responded to people's evolving expectations for security. The results can be felt in people's everyday lives. Efforts to advance the Peaceful China Initiative to a higher level have extended into every urban community and every rural village, reaching the "last mile" of public security. The "Chinese sense of security" also stems from goodwill within society and a sense of civic responsibility found in the social atmosphere: Foreign tourists who lose their phones are able to get them back, and delivery workers report suspicious packages when they spot them. Recently, the positive perception that "Chinese people don't steal phones" has continued to gain traction on overseas social media, with foreign netizens recommending that wherever you travel in the world, look for a Chinese person first if you need someone to take your photo. Under the Peaceful China Initiative, China has not only become one of the world's safest major countries, but has also allowed the world to encounter more and more civic-minded Chinese people. Peaceful China is a light that millions upon millions of Chinese people, secure in their daily lives, shine into a world that is far from peaceful. It is the collective glow of more than 1.4 billion people that forms the strongest and the most dazzling foundation of a peaceful China. The more turbulent the world becomes, the more precious a peaceful China is. As a major country of more than 1.4 billion people, China unwaveringly implements a holistic approach to national security, maintains long-term social stability, and creates an environment in which people can live and work in peace and contentment - that itself is a significant contribution to global peace and security. A peaceful China is not only a shining national calling card, but also a vivid example of China promoting the building of a community with a shared future for humanity. It safeguards the everyday lives of millions of families while contributing Chinese wisdom, Chinese solutions and Chinese strength to global security governance.
